inputs.name: plot_orientation_degrees
inputs.description: Magnetic compass orientation of the primary plot/house frontage (0° = True North, 90° = East, 180° = South, 270° = West). Used to establish the angular reference for the 16 directional zones.

inputs.name: length_width_ratio
inputs.description: Geometric proportion of the house footprint. Classical texts stipulate Caturasra (1:1 square, most auspicious) or Āyata (1:1.25 to 1:1.5 rectangle). Ratios exceeding 1:2 (Kumbha/Vṛtta deformity) suffer severe pranic dissipation.

inputs.name: brahmasthana_status
inputs.description: Status of the central 9 padas in the 81-pada Paramaśāyika grid (or central 4 padas in the 64-pada Maṇḍūka grid). Must remain unencumbered, light-filled, and devoid of vertical shear loads (Marmasthāna protection).

inputs.name: floor_slope_gradient
inputs.description: Overall elevation gradient of the site floor levels. Classical canon mandates natural slope downward toward North-East (Jala-vīthī), preserving elevation in South-West (Pṛthvī-tattva).

inputs.name: aperture_distribution

formula_and_matrix_logic.angular_division_method: Centroid Radial Projection (360° / 16 = 22.5° per zone). The house center (Nābhi) is computed from geometric bounds: C = ((Xmin + Xmax)/2, (Ymin + Ymax)/2). With magnetic tilt θ0, Zone k spans [θ0 + k*22.5° - 11.25°, θ0 + k*22.5° + 11.25°].
formula_and_matrix_logic.pada_vinyasa_correspondence: 81-Pada Paramaśāyika Maṇḍala where the 32 perimeter cells (Paiśāca/Mānuṣa vīthī) and 12 outer intermediate cells are aggregated into 16 directional spokes of 22.5° each, centering on Brahmā (central 9 padas).

scoring_algorithm.composite_formula: Vastu_Index_Percentage = (Sum(w_i * grade_multiplier_i) / Sum(w_i)) * 100. Scaled from 0% (Fatal Dosa throughout) to 100% (Fully aligned classical masterpiece).

formula_and_matrix_logic.marma_protection_doctrine: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 53.55-57: Direct diagonal cords (Vamśas) connecting opposite corners (NE-SW, NW-SE) intersect at 9 Mahā-marmas in Brahmasthāna and 24 secondary marmas. No structural column (Stambha), cross-wall, or waste pipe may intersect these coordinates within a tolerance radius of 1/8th of a pada width.

tools.interpretation: The House Vastu Analyzer evaluates a residential dwelling by projecting a 16-zone radial grid from the architectural centroid (Nābhi) and verifying each functional zone against the 81-pada Paramaśāyika Vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala. Classical Vedic architecture operates on three simultaneous physical and metaphysical laws: (1) The Solar Spectrum Gradient (Saura-krama), capturing soothing germicidal ultraviolet morning rays in the East/North-East while deflecting debilitating infrared thermal heat from the South/South-West; (2) The Geomagnetic Flux (Jaiva-vīthī), guiding positive prāṇic current from the cosmic dipole of the North-East toward the earth sink of the South-West; and (3) The Five Elemental States (Pañcabhūta), ensuring elemental compatibility between structural functions and presiding deities. When these guidelines are satisfied, the living environment acts as a cosmic resonant cavity that stabilizes bio-rhythms, enhances vitality, preserves wealth, and fosters deep familial peace.
tools.variation_note: Textual and regional traditions diverge in significant nuances: (1) The Southern / Kerala school (Manuṣyālaya Candrikā, Śilparatna, Tantrasamuccaya) focuses heavily on the inward-looking Catuḥśālā with a central open sky courtyard (Nāḍumaṭṭam) designed to manage tropical monsoons, and permits an auxiliary kitchen in the North-West (Vāyu-koṇa) if the primary South-East is constrained; (2) The Northern tradition (Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra, Viśvakarma Prakāśa) prioritizes expansive linear halls, perimeter gardens, and fortress-like stone masonry with dedicated underground grain and water vaults; (3) Modern 16-zone systems (as codified by D.N. Shukla from classical texts) refine the traditional 8 directions into 16 subtle psychological sectors of 22.5° each, mapping attributes like Manthana (ESE) and Visarjana (SSW) to address specialized contemporary apartment layouts.

parity_rule.biomechanical_and_spiritual_principle: Ascending human locomotion traditionally begins with the right foot (Dakṣiṇa-pāda). An odd number of steps ensures that the climber lands upon the upper floor destination with the right foot, ensuring muscular equilibrium, biomechanical stability, and psychological victory.

formula_and_matrix_logic.composite_step_rule: A step count is considered optimal ONLY IF it satisfies both conditions: (1) Total_Steps is Odd (Total_Steps % 2 == 1), AND (2) Total_Steps % 3 != 0 (Yields Indu or Jaya). Numbers like 15 and 21, while odd, fail the modulo 3 test (15 % 3 = 0, 21 % 3 = 0) and represent Vyaya. The golden counts are 11, 17, 19, and 23.

tools.interpretation: Staircase Vastu (Sopāna-Vidhi) governs the vertical circulation cores that bridge floor diaphragms and transport energy vertically throughout a multi-storey structure. Mechanically, a staircase represents one of the most substantial dead loads in a building, concentrating severe shear forces and torsional loads at its base stringers. According to the foundational dictum 'Nairṛtye Guru, Īśāne Laghu' (Heavy in the South-West, Light in the North-East), staircases must anchor the terrestrial quadrants (SW, S, W) to counteract overturning moments and preserve the sacred lightness of the North-East and Brahmasthāna. Furthermore, human biomechanics during vertical climbing require that movement follow a clockwise (Pradakṣiṇā) direction, which works cooperatively with the Earth's geomagnetic rotational field. The number of steps must terminate on an odd number so that the ascent concludes with the auspicious right foot, and must yield a remainder of 1 (Indu) or 2 (Jaya) when divided by 3, avoiding the depleting zero remainder of Vyaya (loss).
tools.variation_note: Regional traditions reveal subtle structural adaptations: (1) In Kerala's timber architecture (Manuṣyālaya Candrikā), internal stairs were historically rare in single-storey homes and were built as steep wooden companion ladders (Sopāna-paṭṭikā) leading to attic granaries (Taṭṭu), often oriented externally along the veranda perimeter; (2) In North Indian stone and palace architecture (Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra), broad monumental masonry flights with intermediate resting landings (Sthagitaka) and carved balustrades (Hasti-hasta) were standard, mandating odd counts per individual flight; (3) Folk Vastu often asserts that 'any odd number of steps is acceptable', whereas classical Agamic texts insist on the rigorous modulo 3 filter (excluding 9, 15, and 21 as Vyaya-doṣa); (4) For modern multi-storey buildings with mid-landing turns, classical scholars treat each continuous flight between landings as a distinct energetic movement, while computing the floor-to-floor total for cumulative vibrational harmony.
